item.title: REVIEW: LastPass Review: Solid Features at a Fair Price, But Rivals Offer More Peace of Mind
item.description:
Source: PCMag
LastPass has been in the password management business for well over a decade, and it's best known for polished, easy-to-use apps that work on everything from your laptop to your smartwatch. It autofills smoothly and includes free data breach monitoring on every plan. It's easy to like LastPass, except for one thing: its security record. Most recently, in June 2026, hackers used stolen LastPass OAuth tokens from a third-party provider to access customer data. I'm not ready to say LastPass can't be trusted. The company has a long track record and has made real security improvements following past incidents. But the latest breach shows those improvements haven't closed every gap, which is why I've lowered its score by half a point since my last review. LastPass remains a capable, easy-to-use option, but Proton Pass is still our Editors’ Choice for free password management, and NordPass is our top pick for its affordable, full-featured personal and business plans. LastPass offers three different plans for consumers: Free, Premium, and Families. The Free edition is limited to one account on either a computer or mobile devices (including phones, smartwatches, and tablets). With the free tier, you can share credentials one-on-one and monitor your accounts for dark web activity, but storage is limited to 50MB, and it doesn't include emergency access features. While LastPass's free plan has limits, you can try the Premium plan at no charge for up to 30 days. After that, a LastPass Premium subscription costs $36 per year. In addition to the free version's features, you gain access to your vault across all of your devices, one-to-many password sharing, passkey storage, advanced multi-factor options (biometric and YubiKey support), access to the LastPass Authenticator smartwatch app for watchOS or Wear OS, emergency access, priority tech support, and 1GB of encrypted file storage. There's also a Plus plan for $7 per month or $84 annually that, in addition to the premium version of the password manager, includes unlimited access to LastPass VPN for up to 10 devices. This subscription is only for Windows devices. The top tier for non-business accounts is LastPass Family ($48 annually). LastPass Family subscribers get six LastPass Premium licenses, unlimited shared folders, authentication via hardware security keys, and access to the LastPass family dashboard. LastPass plans are about average compared with competitors. For example, NordPass is $35.88 for an annual subscription, and RoboForm is $29.88 per year. LastPass costs significantly less than Dashlane, which, at $64.99, is the most expensive password manager I've tested, but it includes VPN access as part of the base-level personal subscription plan. LastPass Plus includes VPN access, but only with the $84 Plus plan (and it only works with Windows devices). LastPass is available as Android and iOS apps, plus extensions for Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera, and Safari. It also offers universal installer apps for Linux, macOS, and Windows that automatically install extensions across all your devices' browsers. As mentioned above, you can access LastPass via the watchOS and Wear OS apps. To sign up for LastPass, visit the website, enter an email address, and create a strong master password. Only you know your master password, so if you forget it, LastPass cannot help you access your vault. Once you're in your vault, it's time to tick off items on a to-do list, which is LastPass's version of a tutorial for new customers. If you've never used a password manager before, I recommend using the list to familiarize yourself with the app's features and to practice generating and autofilling passwords on websites. If you've used a password manager before, you'll want to upload the existing login list that you exported from your old password manager or browser extension to your LastPass vault. To import your existing passwords, open the web vault in a browser window, and click on Advanced Options at the bottom left of the screen, then click Import. LastPass can import from several competing products, including 1Password, Bitwarden, Dashlane, KeePass, and RoboForm. If your old password manager is not on the list, you can upload your credentials in CSV format. LastPass also imports passwords from Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Internet Explorer, Opera, and Safari. If you've been saving your passwords in physical notebooks or in a spreadsheet on your computer, LastPass offers instructions for transferring these credentials, too. I like that LastPass's on-screen instructions guide customers through the setup process in a way that is instructive without being too simplistic. For example, after you've imported a list of passwords, an on-screen prompt offers a helpful suggestion: Visit your security dashboard to see whether you uploaded any breached, reused, or weak passwords. I'll dig into the password audit system later in the review, but first, we need to look at how LastPass treats customer data. Before I review and test a password manager, I ask company representatives about its privacy and security practices. For insight into LastPass's privacy policies, read the company's answers to my questions below. Has your company ever had a security breach? Yes. If so, when? Please provide dates. 2015 (GoTo was breached), and in 2022. You can find a dedicated resource detailing what happened, what data was exposed, and the steps we’ve taken to harden our security since at LastPass.com. Reviewer's note: In June 2026, through a breach at Klue, a third-party service provider, hackers obtained LastPass OAuth tokens, then used them to access customer data. Read the company's response here, as it did not mention the 2026 event in its response to us. What was exposed in the breach? 2015 - Before being acquired by LogMeIn, Inc. (now known as GoTo), GoTo experienced an incident in 2015 where a hard drive was stolen from one of their data centers. This drive did not include users’ vaults but did include unencrypted data related to their accounts. LastPass was a product under the company GoTo in 2015 therefore LastPass, the company, didn’t experience a security breach in 2015. 2022 - LastPass disclosed that a threat actor had gained access to a cloud storage environment used for backups and exfiltrated both encrypted and unencrypted customer data. What unencrypted information does the password manager store in customer vaults? No data is ever stored unencrypted in user vaults. Encryption and decryption are ONLY performed on the end-user’s device. LastPass does not have access to or store the master password which derives the encryption key used to encrypt/decrypt customer data. This is aligned to our Zero-knowledge principles. LastPass customer vault data is encrypted using AES-256 on a per-user basis (meaning every user’s encryption keys are unique). Encrypted fields within the vault include usernames, passwords, website names, notes, payment cards, addresses, bank accounts, item and folder names, secure notes, etc. What is the company's policy regarding selling or sharing customer data with third parties? At LastPass, we always strive to limit the types and categories of data that is collected from, and processed on behalf of, our users to include only data which is necessary to achieve the purpose(s) for which it was collected - in other words, we have measures and policies in place designed to ensure that we only collect and process data that we believe is necessary to provide our users with a world-class service. LastPass does not sell end user data to third parties – including any vault data. Under some US state data protection laws, our use of third-party cookies on our website for advertising purposes may constitute a “sale”. We specifically inform visitors of the use of those technologies within our cookie banner, and, depending on the visitor’s location, cookies are only deployed after a visitor opts-in to their use. Furthermore, we afford individuals to manage their privacy rights by changing opting-out of the sale or sharing of their personal data through the cookie banner, the Cookie Preferences link present at the bottom of our webpage or submitting a request through our Individual Rights Management Portal. How does your company respond to requests for customer information from governments and law enforcement? LastPass will not disclose customer information to governments or law enforcement unless presented with a valid warrant, subpoena, court order, or equivalent legal process. Each request is considered on a case-by-case basis, and LastPass is committed to responsibly balancing our legal and regulatory obligations with the commitments to promote public safety and user privacy, which may include attempting to narrow requests that it deems excessively broad, request further clarification if the nature of the investigation is ambiguous, or contest the request for other reasons. Additional information can be found in the LastPass Law Enforcement Request Guidelines. Further, due to our zero-knowledge security model, we do not possess, and cannot obtain, the master password needed to be able to decrypt any encrypted customer vault data. Therefore, we cannot provide such information in response to a government request. Overall, LastPass’s answers match the company's privacy policy. Always review the privacy policies of all apps to learn how companies collect, sell, or store your data. Premium and Families account holders may be able to forgo entering a master password every time they login by setting up a passwordless entry method, such as a code from the LastPass authenticator app, biometrics from Windows Hello, or a FIDO2-certified hardware security key. Head over to your account settings menu to enable passwordless logins. LastPass will ask for your phone number to verify your identity via SMS. I chose not to provide a phone number for this evaluation and opted to use a Yubico Security Key C NFC as my primary login method. I was able to attach my security key to the account, but I needed to add another authentication factor to complete the setup. I attempted to use Apple Passwords and Google Authenticator for this step, but LastPass did not acknowledge these commonly used apps. Instead, I was prompted to download another app, the LastPass Authenticator, to complete this task. It shouldn't be necessary to download an additional company app and keep it on my phone to log into my account without a password, so I can't recommend this login method. You should still use multi-factor authentication to secure your vault, though. That way, anyone who guesses or steals your master password won't be able to access your credentials without you or your device being present. Each time you log in, you'll need to supply a time-based one-time password (TOTP) generated by the app (essentially a six-digit code that typically changes every 30 seconds) in addition to your master password. You can designate your phone or desktop computer as a Trusted Device in the Account Settings menu, which means you won't need to authenticate on those devices for 30 days. Unfortunately, LastPass's MFA setup isn't super user-friendly, either. First, head over to Account Settings > Multi-Factor Options in the Web Vault. The available authentication methods depend on your subscription tier. Free subscribers can use Duo Security, Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, older YubiKeys that support Yubico OTP, or the aforementioned LastPass Authenticator app. Families plan subscribers can use a newer hardware security key as an MFA method. Choose your authentication method, tap Edit, then choose Yes to enable it. Next, connect your app to your LastPass account by scanning a QR code. Choose barcode in the Edit menu to access the QR code. Choose private key to manually enter a token in your authenticator app. Other password managers offer streamlined, straightforward MFA enrollment systems, so this is an area where LastPass could improve. The LastPass Security Dashboard calculates a score based on the strength of your passwords and whether you have enabled multi-factor authentication. Click on the View button to see a list of all the passwords in your vault. LastPass rates each password's strength and identifies potential risks. The password audit tool identified reused and missing passwords in my vault and recommended changing those credentials. However, LastPass did not flag short (under 10 characters) or easily guessable passwords, which isn't great. While Keeper offers data breach monitoring as a paid add-on and NordPass limits it to paid subscribers, LastPass offers it at all service levels and automatically enrolls customers at signup. Free customers can monitor up to 10 email addresses, while paid subscribers can monitor 200 email addresses. You can turn data breach monitoring on or off at any time from the Security Center window. I tested LastPass using the web vault, iOS app, and Chrome browser extension. The LastPass web vault was easy to navigate, and you can change the default view to display website icons or a list of your credentials. Replaying passwords stored in the LastPass vault worked as expected. I also didn't have any trouble creating new credentials and saving them in my LastPass vault. I was able to save passkeys in my LastPass vault with just a click, too. Remember that passkeys are device-specific, so if you save a passkey for an account using the browser extension or web vault, you'll need to create a different passkey for that website when you try to sign in using your phone. If you have problems while autofilling your logins or saving new ones, go to Autofill Settings in the Advanced Options section of the web vault to see whether the domain you're on is on your Never save list. If you're unable to autofill your logins using the mobile app, scroll down the Mobile Apps section of this review to learn how to turn on autofilling for your device. All LastPass password generators create 16-character-long credentials by default. I recommend changing the settings to create long, strong passwords of at least 20 characters. Free LastPass customers can set up one-to-one sharing, but Premium and Family subscribers can share one item with several others. Those who pay for a Family account can share an unlimited number of folders. To share a password, click the sharing icon and enter the recipient's email address. Recipients who already use LastPass will receive a notification that a new share has arrived; others will get an email explaining how to create an account and accept the share. The recipient can use the shared item to log in. The person sharing the password can manage the recipient's access to the credential via the Sharing Center in the web vault. You can manage whether the recipient can view the password while they have access to it, and also relinquish access to credentials others have shared with you, or cut off others with whom you've shared passwords. You can store multiple addresses, bank account details, and payment card numbers in your vault, along with personal and contact information. I was able to use LastPass to fill in web form data on a few websites, and was impressed by the warning that appears when you opt to fill in forms using data from your LastPass vault. LastPass reminds you that you are sharing sensitive data with a third party, which may be enough to make you stop, reflect, and consider whether you are being phished or otherwise scammed. Secure notes are a way to store data in your LastPass account that doesn’t fit into any other categories, such as text notes and file attachments. Premium LastPass subscribers get 1 GB of online storage; free customers are limited to 50 MB. Other password managers have beefed up file storage options in an effort to become "everything managers". For example, Proton Pass Plus subscribers can store up to 10 GB in vaults, and that storage increases to 500 GB with a Proton Unlimited subscription. The Emergency Access feature lets you designate one or more contacts who can access your passwords in the event of your untimely demise. This feature is only for paid accounts. Emergency Access in LastPass works similarly to the equivalent features in Dashlane, Keeper, and Proton Pass. You enter your recipient's email address and define a waiting period. Recipients must install LastPass and accept your connection request. Now, if something happens to you, the recipient simply requests access to your account. Here's where the waiting period comes in. Suppose your trusted recipient decides to jump the gun and get your passwords before you've kicked the bucket. The initial access request triggers a notification, and you can deny it at any time during the waiting period. In a real emergency, your recipient automatically gains access once that time has elapsed. Clicking Emergency Access opens two pages: People I Trust (your password heirs) and People Who Trust Me (those who've made you their emergency access contact). You can delete anyone from the list or change the waiting period on the People I Trust page. You can bow out of the emergency access role on the People Who Trust Me page. The Android and iOS editions include all of LastPass’s web features, including a password generator, emergency access, a security dashboard, and a sharing center. The mobile app includes another "to-do list" tutorial, but you can dismiss or mute it with a single tap. You may need to designate LastPass as your primary password manager in your device's settings menu for autofill to work. To do this on Android, go to Settings > Privacy. If you have an Apple device, go to Settings > General > Autofill and Passwords. These menu paths will differ depending on whether you're using older or newer versions of the operating system. Overall, I didn't have any problems capturing new passwords or replaying old ones using the LastPass app for iOS. The Security section of the app provides access to a unique password hygiene tool: a Password Challenge, which scans your vault for reused or weak passwords. As mentioned, I keep a few insecure credentials in my test vault, but the challenge tool did not flag the passwords. Free account holders can troubleshoot their tech issues via the recently revamped LastPass self-service website. From there, you can fill out a form to be contacted by a support agent. LastPass also has a chatbot on its support website. Business, Family, and Premium personal account customers can request phone support from a LastPass support agent. Business and Business Max accounts can get an account customer success manager. Deleting the account I created to test LastPass apps was uncomplicated. In a web browser, I navigated to the Account page and chose the Delete option. After clicking through several pop-ups to confirm I really wanted to delete the account and its associated vaults, I was able to do so. LastPass for Business has three service tiers, each priced per employee: Teams costs $51 annually, Business costs $84 annually, and Business Max costs $132 annually, an increase from its previous price of $108 per year. A Teams account is best for small teams or lean startups, and includes employee management via the admin console, shared folders, TOTP passcode generation, and limited security policies. Small businesses with several employees or medium-sized businesses may want to upgrade to a LastPass Business account, which includes free Families accounts for employees, Group management tools, SSO integration for up to three apps, an SSO portal for employees, and additional customizable security policies. A Business Max account includes AI monitoring tools to block and track employees' access to apps and software via work accounts, advanced MFA options, unlimited SSO integrations, organization-wide SaaS protection and visibility, and passwordless authentication across all endpoints. LastPass makes it easy for administrators to see who is following password policies on the job and who is not. For example, the admin dashboard shows the company’s enrollment rate with the password manager, employee activity, and average password security score. Employees receive a vault to store their work-related credentials. An administrator can see all employees invited to use the password manager, when each employee last used the software, whether each employee enabled multi-factor authentication (MFA) for their account, password security scores, and other options. Admins can integrate SSO, MFA, and password-less apps from the Applications section of the Admin console. The app also supports federation with ADFS, Azure AD, Google Workspace, and Okta, so employees can access LastPass using their existing corporate credentials in their current workspaces. Eliminating the need to remember another password could make password manager adoption more attractive to employees. As mentioned above, LastPass's business plans include a free Families account for every employee to encourage vigilant password practices at home. The LastPass Families plan data is separate from the Business data. LastPass has a zero-knowledge security model, so only the employees know their passwords. If an employee leaves the company, their Families account unlinks from the Business account. The former employee can either buy a Families plan or convert the account to a Free account. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. LastPass offers polished, easy-to-use apps for nearly every platform, and its onboarding tutorial is one of the best I've seen, guiding new users through setup without talking down to them. Free data breach monitoring on every plan is another standout, since many competitors charge for it. But a password manager's first job is keeping your data safe, and LastPass's repeated security incidents, most recently in June 2026, are hard to overlook from a company with its long history, so I've lowered its score by half a star. Ultimately, Proton Pass remains our top pick for free password management, while NordPass earns high marks for its full-featured, competitively priced personal and business plans. STILL ON THE FENCE? I review privacy tools like hardware security keys, password managers, private messaging apps, and ad-blocking software. I also report on online scams and offer advice to families and individuals about staying safe on the internet. Before joining PCMag, I wrote about tech and video games for CNN, Fanbyte, Mashable, The New York Times, and TechRadar. I also worked at CNN International, where I did field producing and reporting on sports that are popular with worldwide audiences. In addition to the categories below, I exclusively cover ad blockers, authenticator apps, hardware security keys, and private messaging apps.

item.title: SALES: 11 best Airbnbs in Budapest have panoramic river views, rooftop terraces and bags of historic charm
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Frozen in time yet roaring with energy, Budapest promises a memorable city break like no other. The Hungarian capital is centred around its beloved river, the Danube, which separates the calmer Buda region from vibrant Pest. Spilling out from both sides of the riverbank, there’s a plethora of stunning gothic architecture and UNESCO world heritage sites to uncover, as well as an eccentric nightlife scene in the notorious ruin bars downtown. Known as the City of Spas, Budapest has also earned a name for itself as a wellbeing destination, drawing crowds for its therapeutic waters powered by over 100 natural springs. With so much to explore, you’ll need a base from where to decompress – and what’s more relaxing than a homey Budapest Airbnb? While there are plenty of gorgeous hotels across the city, the many Airbnbs in Budapest offer an authenticity that can’t be beat. Below, our picks of the best Airbnbs in Budapest to book for your next visit. item.title: REVIEW: RoboForm Review: A Budget-Friendly Password Manager That Gets the Basics Right
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Sticky notes and recycled passwords are an invitation to hackers. A password manager is the fix, and RoboForm is one of the most affordable ways to get a good one. For less than $30 a year, it syncs unlimited passwords and passkeys across all your devices, monitors the web for data breaches, and adds handy emergency access and sharing tools. NordPass, our Editors’ Choice winner, offers more features overall, but RoboForm costs less and is well worth considering if you want reliable password management on a budget. RoboForm offers a free subscription, but it's pretty bare-bones compared with competitors such as Bitwarden, LogMeOnce, and Proton Pass, which offer unlimited password storage on all platforms and password syncing across all devices. RoboForm's free password manager is limited to one device and doesn't include features like web vault access or shared folders. Free customers can only get help from RoboForm's support team via email. You can try out RoboForm's premium subscription for free for 30 days with a trial personal account. Once your free trial expires, the premium perks disappear, and the vault reverts to a free account, with the device limitation applied. If you're ready to pay for a new password manager, RoboForm is excellent value for a low price, as the premium plan is $29.88 annually and adds password syncing across all your devices, data breach monitoring for up to 5 emails, emergency access, sharing rights, and customer support via email, live chat, and phone. A Family subscription is $47.76 per year for five premium accounts. RoboForm's pricing is on par with or below that of much of the competition, as NordPass's premium plans start at $35.88 and 1Password's start at $59.88. RoboForm also offers competitively priced business plans that, like the personal plans, come with a free trial period. The primary Business tier is $39.96 per employee, per year. Enterprise-level pricing is available upon request. I'll dig into the business tier features later in the review. RoboForm has browser extensions for Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari. It also offers desktop clients for Mac and Windows, as well as apps for Android and iOS. To sign up, visit RoboForm's website or download one of the apps and create an account. After that, create a strong, unique master password that you'll use to log into your account in the future. With RoboForm, if you forget your master password, you can recover access to your vault using a device that was previously enrolled for MFA and is still logged into your account, which is helpful. Throughout the testing period, I was impressed with RoboForm's commitment to helping customers get the most out of the app. I kept noticing tips and hints for maintaining password hygiene sprinkled throughout. For example, if you tap or hover over a credential with a weak password, RoboForm offers instructions for changing the password in your vault and on the associated website, as well as video tutorials for all the app's features to help people new to password managers. RoboForm can import credentials from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Opera. The app can also import them from competing password managers, including 1Password, Bitwarden, Dashlane, Enpass, Kaspersky, Keeper, LastPass, Proton Pass, NordPass, True Key, and the now-defunct Myki app. Switching to RoboForm from your old password manager? You can upload an unbranded CSV file saved from a different password management system. Before I test a password manager, I send the company a set of questions about its privacy and security practices. I do this because I want you to have plenty of information about the companies handling your data. After all, what happens to your data if the company gets hacked? RoboForm's responses to my questions are in italics below. Has your company ever had a security breach? No. What unencrypted information does the password manager store in user vaults? None. All user data inside the RoboForm account is encrypted, and we cannot access it. What is the company's policy regarding selling or sharing customer data with third parties? We do not sell user data. How does your company respond to requests for user information from governments and law enforcement? Requests for user information must be for specific account(s) and be served to us through a court order. From there, we would review the request for validity and comply in accordance with US law. RoboForm's answers to my questions match the company's privacy policy. I encourage anyone looking for a new password manager to browse privacy policies to learn more about how companies collect, sell, or store user data. Though you need to designate a master password when you sign up, you don't have to enter it every time you log in. That's because RoboForm supports passwordless vault logins for its apps and browser extensions using either biometrics or a PIN on your mobile device. RoboForm can also generate a passkey that you keep on a hardware security key or other device and use to login instead of a password. After signing in to your vault, click Settings, then open the Login and Security menu to set up your multi-factor authentication (MFA) method. Activate the appropriate toggle in the MFA section, complete the provided instructions, and sign up. You can authenticate your identity using another trusted device, such as a smartphone secured with biometrics or a passcode, or with an authenticator app, email address (activated by default), hardware security key, or SMS. I used Apple Passwords' built-in authenticator for my test account and logged in without any problems. Keep in mind that you can also use RoboForm as an authenticator app for your accounts. There's a form field for each vault credential for that account's MFA token. RoboForm provides password hygiene analysis in the Security Center, so you can tell if you're using the same one too often, or if your passwords are easily guessed or hacked. As I mentioned earlier in the review, I like that RoboForm provides actionable advice for improving your passwords within the Security Center and identifies duplicate or weak passwords in your vault. RoboForm offers data breach monitoring for up to five email addresses for paid accounts. Many other password managers, like Dashlane, NordPass, and Proton Pass, also keep this vital online health checkup tool behind a paywall, so RoboForm isn't unusual. Bitwarden offers free data breach monitoring for all customers, which is ideal. RoboForm's data breach reports are from haveibeenpwned's database. I liked the amount of detail in each report. You can find out when a breach occurred, what types of data were taken, and, in some reports, the company's response. Reports are divided into lists of critical or non-critical breaches. I recommend looking closely at both lists. Critical breaches involve a stolen password, while non-critical breaches can involve anything from your credit card data to your phone number and government ID information. You can reach this section by navigating to the Settings menu and opening Devices and Activity. Here, you'll find a list of all the devices authorized to access your RoboForm account, along with timestamped login activity. If you see a device you don't recognize or other suspicious activity, remove access and change your account password right away. Anti-phishing protection is enabled by default. Phishing scammers often buy commonly mistyped domains (like amaxon.com) to trick people into giving them their credit card numbers or other personal information. When you're using the app or a browser extension, RoboForm will notify you if it appears that you're entering sensitive personal data or financial information on a website with a domain that doesn't match the one in your vault. I tested RoboForm using the web vault, the Chrome browser extension, the Android app, and the iOS app. The apps are easy to navigate. After I imported my test lists, buttons featuring icons for each login on the list appeared in the web vault, which is a nice touch. I've seen similar user interfaces in many mobile password manager apps, and RoboForm offers this highly accessible layout by default. If you prefer a file tree or like the look of smaller icons, you can change the view by clicking the view options on the right side of the window. You can switch to dark mode in the Account menu, which changes the background from light gray to black. I like that the traditional folder system view includes a column showing your password strength. When you hover your mouse over the password hygiene alert, RoboForm urges you to replace weak passwords with stronger ones. Access to your logins, bookmarks, and any notes you create is via a menu on the left side of the screen. A menu at the bottom left lets you use a password generator, access RoboForm's authenticator, check your password hygiene via the Security Center, share passwords, and designate emergency access rules for your account. The RoboForm browser extension worked as expected in testing. I was able to access my imported passwords and log in to my test accounts with one click. Capturing existing credentials, generating new passwords, and saving new logins was also painless. You can choose how you want RoboForm to fill in your credentials. Navigate to the Settings menu in the browser extension or the web vault, then open the Autofill section. From there, you can decline to autofill credentials, have RoboForm prompt you each time there's an opportunity to enter a password, or choose to have RoboForm autofill without your input. Though it requires an extra step, I don't recommend auto-filling your credentials without notifications, since criminals can exploit this feature to steal your passwords. It's nice to have options. Overall, I liked the browser extension's credential capture-and-replay system. Using the RoboForm password generator, users can set a password length of up to 512 characters and choose whether to include capital and lowercase letters, digits, hexadecimal characters, and symbols. The default password generation length with RoboForm is 22 characters. You can also create passphrases up to 8 words long that include capital letters and numbers. You can save passkeys in your RoboForm vault, too. A passkey credential entry looks similar to a traditional username+password credential. As mentioned earlier in the review, you can also create a passkey and save it on a different device if you want to login to RoboForm without using your master password. RoboForm started as a form-filling utility, so it's not surprising that entering my information into RoboForm was easy. To store information you'll frequently enter on web forms, such as your address, banking details, business information, credit cards, car information, and passport number, click your name in the vault dashboard to open the information type list. I had no trouble filling out forms around the web using the data stored in my vault. If you need to store other kinds of information in your vault, like a Wi-Fi password, your driver's license number, or your pet's birthday wish list, you can create small text documents in the SafeNotes section of the app. You can send and share SafeNotes to other RoboForm customers, but anyone else will need to sign up for a RoboForm account to view your SafeNotes. I'll dig into the differences between sending and sharing in the next section. Unlike many competing password managers, RoboForm does not allow customers to store files in their vault. For example, NordPass and Proton Pass upgraded the paid password management tiers to allow customers to upload files and keep them in vaults. File storage has been a long-standing feature in Dashlane, and Keeper's Family plan includes 10 gigabytes of storage. Paid account holders can share individual passwords, the aforementioned SafeNotes, and two credential folders. Sharing individual passwords with other RoboForm users is easy; just click on the three dots next to the vault entry, then choose Share. Enter the email address associated with the person's RoboForm account. If your intended recipient does not use RoboForm, enter their email address, and they will receive an email from RoboForm asking them to create a free account so that they can access the credentials. You can designate up to five recipients per login and remove access whenever you wish. Changing the password after you revoke access is probably wise, so other people can't continue accessing the account. You cannot designate access levels when sharing individual credentials, which is not great. Shared Folders are handy if you have a friend or hobby group that shares service credentials, or if your family needs to share a few logins to pay bills or access shared online accounts. You can choose to give people different levels of access to credentials within the folder. Your fellow RoboForm customer can either only use the credential to login, edit the credential, or get full access to the password. It's a clunky solution for password sharing. Other password managers make sharing credentials with family and friends a little easier. For example, in addition to in-app sharing, Keeper offers a One-Time Share option that lets customers send passwords via AirDrop, QR codes, or SMS to people who aren't on the same platform. If a stranger intercepts the link, it's useless; the password is accessible only on the device it was sent to. NordPass lets you set expiration dates for shared passwords, so you don't have to worry about forgetting to revoke someone's access. You can also adjust individual permission levels for each credential, giving customers more power over who can access their logins. No one gets out of this coil alive, so it's best to prepare for your demise while you can. Planning for your digital legacy is a wise time investment, and most password managers include an emergency access option that lets family or friends close out your online accounts after you die. Paying RoboForm subscribers can designate an emergency contact who can access their credentials. RoboForm allows users to designate a time-out period, which is the time between an emergency designee's request to access your logins and when you must grant or deny that access. If you're worried about someone trying to access your logins while you're still with us, you can set a long period (up to 30 days). You must invite your designee to create a free RoboForm account before designating them as your emergency contact. I tried out RoboForm's Android and iOS apps, and both look good and performed well in testing. Screenshots are disabled by default for Android customers, but you can turn them back on via the Settings menu if you're inclined. The app includes a built-in browser that includes an ad blocker, private mode, and reader mode, just like one of your favorite mainstream browsers. I didn't have any trouble entering my credentials or data in the mobile app, which is great. The autofill was smooth; just remember to designate RoboForm as your preferred password manager in your device's Settings menu. If you have the latest version of iOS (26.2 or later), RoboForm can generate passwords within iOS apps and automatically save them to your RoboForm vault. Free account holders can email the RoboForm support team for help. Paid personal and business accounts can contact the company via live chat Monday through Friday, 6 a.m. to 8 p.m., and on weekends, 6 am to 6 pm, US Eastern time. You can also troubleshoot your issue by reading articles and watching videos in the RoboForm Help Center. Deleting my RoboForm account was drama-free and very easy. I just visited the Account and Data section of my profile in the Settings menu, scrolled to the bottom of the page, and clicked the Delete My RoboForm Account button. Business owners can sign up for a free trial to try out RoboForm's Business edition. After the trial ends, the service, though often discounted, costs $39.96 per year per user. The plan includes activity logs, dark web monitoring and alerts, password hygiene reports, password sharing, role-based access control, single sign-on (SSO) integration, customizable security policies, and other business-focused features. RoboForm also offers enterprise-level password management for large businesses. Both plans include a dedicated account manager and priority customer support. After logging in to my admin account, I added a test account to my fake company to see the level of access an admin has in RoboForm. I like that you can designate group-based credential access, and generating reports for specific users or groups of employees is very helpful. Admins can also restrict access to the corporate RoboForm account to specific IPs, so employees can access only their credentials while they're in the office or at home. Admins can also protect company data by limiting employees' exporting and importing capabilities within the app and blocking RoboForm use on certain apps or websites. The Business features are very helpful; however, I have one minor privacy quibble with the dark web monitoring feature, as it could be invasive. As an admin, I could see all of the details of my fake, hapless employees' data breach reports, which is fine if they're using a work email address, but if you have contractors on staff, or anyone else who is using an email address that they also use for personal accounts, well, you're liable to know more than you want to know about your employees' online habits over the years. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. It isn't perfect: The free plan is limited to a single device, sharing passwords outside of shared folders is clunky, and you can't store files in your vault the way you can with Dashlane, NordPass, or Proton Pass. item.title: SALES: 8 best Afghan restaurants in London for your next culinary adventure
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Afghan food is undoubtedly delicious. From delicate mantu dumplings stuffed with minced meat and smothered in garlicky yoghurt to enormous platters of Kabuli Pulao, fragrant rice piled high with tender lamb and sweet raisins, the cuisine is full of rich flavours. Then there are the smoky charcoal-grilled kebabs and gently spiced, slow-cooked stews, best scooped up with freshly baked naan and washed down with glasses of doogh, a salty yoghurt drink flavoured with mint. Yet despite all this, Afghan restaurants remain relatively overlooked in a city that prides itself on eating its way around the world. A handful of newer openings are beginning to change that. In Leyton, recently opened Azra has embraced the sort of polished interiors and small-plate dining that Londoners have become rather fond of. Elsewhere, Cue Point is taking a more unconventional approach, combining traditional Afghan flavours with the smoky, slow-cooked techniques of Texan barbecue. Many of the capital's older Afghan restaurants, however, are found in areas with established Afghan communities, particularly Harrow in northwest London, with others scattered across Islington and Holloway. These are often reassuringly old-school affairs, where Afghan flags hang proudly on the walls, televisions chatter away in the background and the furniture might not have received much attention from an interior designer. But in an age when Instagrammable interiors have become, rather unfairly, something of a prerequisite for a good restaurant, don't be put off by a little decorative eccentricity. The cooking is superb, with enormous portions and family recipes passed down through generations. From neighbourhood stalwarts to smart new openings, these are the best Afghan restaurants in London.

item.title: REVIEW: Everything You Need in Your First Laptop Without the Luxury Price Tag
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
The PC market has never been more diverse, and utterly punishing on the wallet, thanks to the AI boom and resultant price inflation we are seeing in 2026. Most people shopping for a pocket-friendly laptop don’t necessarily care about core counts, clock speeds, or refresh rates. They want something that opens Chrome quickly, plays Netflix without stuttering, and survives a few years of assignments. For a long time, that was too much to ask. I’ve tested plenty of budget laptops that felt tired out of the box, with plastic that flexed under my palms and fans that roared every time I opened a few tabs. Most of them felt noticeably slower within a year. The Dell 15 breaks that cycle entirely. By applying professional-grade engineering standards to an entry-level category, Dell delivers laboratory-tested durability, smart cooling, and all-day reliability. It stands out as a uniquely practical investment for anyone buying their maiden machine and wanting elite performance without paying a fortune. In my experience, cheap laptops rarely die because the processor can’t keep up. They die from everyday abuse. A backpack slips off a bus seat, or the hinge loosens after months of being tossed around in a bag. Most budget machines aren’t built for that. Dell says the Dell 15 has passed 15 MIL-STD-810H tests covering drops, vibration, humidity, temperature swings, and high altitude. These are Dell’s own tests, and they suggest the chassis will handle a rougher routine than most laptops at this price. If you’re a first-time buyer nervous about taking a laptop outside, that’s reassuring. Durability is only one part of the picture. If you use your laptop for online banking or store personal documents on it, security matters just as much. The Dell 15 includes a hardware Trusted Platform Module (TPM) chip, which stores encryption keys separately from the rest of the system. That makes your encrypted files and sign-in credentials much harder to tamper with, right out of the box. Older budget laptops often make working from a sofa or bed uncomfortable. When air vents are blocked, cooling fans whine, the underside gets uncomfortably hot, and performance throttles, turning basic tasks into a choppy mess. The Dell 15 solves this with adaptive thermals. Built-in motion sensors work behind the scenes to recognize where the laptop is resting. On a flat desk, the system optimizes airflow and power delivery to prioritize sustained processor output for intensive multitasking and media streaming. When you move the notebook to your lap, the system instantly recalibrates. It gently shifts power limits and fan curves to keep the underside pleasantly cool and make fan noise practically silent. Powered by an Intel Core 3 processor and Windows 11, this system delivers responsive everyday performance, fast application launches and smooth multitasking across your most-used apps and browser tabs. Good hardware design is about how comfortably a device functions during hours of writing or streaming. Opening the lid reveals an expansive 15.3-inch Full High-Definition screen bordered by slim bezels. This wide display offers ample space to dock two full windows side by side, allowing you to reference research notes while drafting an essay or check bank statements while updating an expense sheet. Underneath the screen sits a spacious, ergonomic keyboard with a full numeric keypad on the right. If you study accounting, manage household budgets, or enter numbers, having dedicated numeric keys saves valuable time. Most portable laptops drop the numeric pad to cut costs, but Dell kept it for everyday convenience. Battery endurance is equally reassuring, but ExpressCharge technology stands out. We have all had moments of forgetfulness, stepping away from a laptop without plugging it in and finding a dead battery before a meeting, which usually spells panic. With ExpressCharge, the Dell 15 powers up from empty to about 80% capacity in an hour using the included adapter while the machine is asleep or turned off. A brief coffee break gives you plenty of power to tackle your day without feeling tethered to a wall outlet. Verified Owner Satisfaction and Eco-Friendly Build When I look at budget laptops, spec sheets can only tell us so much. But what really matters is how they treat you once you unbox them and put them to work. The Dell 15 has quietly built a strong reputation in that department, earning a solid 4.5-star rating across 4,274 verified customer reviews. Everyday users consistently talk about the balanced feel, smooth multitasking, quick wake-up times, and sharp screen, making it easier to trust when you are shopping for your first computer. It is also rare to see a budget laptop pay this much attention to the planet. Dell builds sustainability into the notebook’s core, using 30% post-consumer recycled plastics, ENERGY STAR certification for energy efficiency, and EPEAT Gold registration for eco-friendly manufacturing. Plus, fully renewable, plant-based box materials round out the design so you can easily recycle the packaging when you are done. Choosing Between the Dell 15 and Dell 14 While the Dell 15 is an ideal daily workhorse for home desks, dorms, and stationary office setups, your lifestyle may call for something more compact. If your daily routine involves moving between lecture halls, working in neighborhood cafes, or traveling light with just a slim messenger bag, the Dell 14 offers a smaller, more portable alternative. Both laptops are designed for everyday productivity, but the choice comes down to whether you prefer the extra screen space and dedicated numeric keypad of the Dell 15 or the portability of the Dell 14. Buying your first computer shouldn’t feel like an intimidating puzzle, and getting what you actually need shouldn’t mean breaking the bank. Skip the marketing hype, and you’re left with a reliable setup that handles daily demands, locks down your data, and survives being tossed into a backpack every morning. Rounding it off, the Dell 15 stands out because it focuses entirely on real-world utility. By blending rugged build quality, smart cooling that keeps your lap comfortable, and practical extras like a numeric pad, it proves you can get a machine you can count on without overspending.

item.title: REVIEW: Aomei Backupper Standard 8.5 review: Free and surprisingly capable backup
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
- Problematic recovery disk creation and boot The startlingly capable Standard version of Aomei Backupper will meet most users’ needs for zero coin and only a few “buy me” nags. But the boot media is difficult to create and requires lowering BIOS security standards. This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Prices Today: Aomei Backupper Standard To keep essential data backed up, most users can easily get away with using Windows integrated File History, and various freebies. One of the shining lights among said freebies is Aomei’s Backupper Standard. Windows’ own disaster recovery options aren’t particularly easy or reliable, hence the boon of a program such as Aomei Backupper Standard that facilitates free and reliable system recovery. Alas, Backupper Standard needed a bit of help. I had to employ the venerable and equally free third-party boot-disk creation tool (Rufus 4.8) to create Backupper recovery media that would boot successfully on my test systems. Consider that worthy utility a necessary adjunct to Backupper Standard. Read on to learn more, then see our roundup of the best Windows backup software for comparison. What are Aomei Backupper Standard 8.5’s features? I did a comprehensive comparison of Backupper Standard and Backupper Professional (before I discovered the cheat sheet) to discern which features were and were not implemented in the Standard version. I was quite surprised at the overall functionality that’s included. All the basics from the paid version are there: file/folder backup, system/drive/partition imaging, one-way sync with the ability to schedule all of them. Incremental and differential backup are supported, as is disaster recovery. Though, as mentioned, I ran into a bit of an issue creating the PE recovery disk (Linux is no longer offered). Ultimate success was mine, but read the performance section carefully for clues on how. Backupper Professional features that are missing in Standard include: mirroring, two-way, and real-time sync; culling of backups (removing old unneeded files to make room for more); system clone and partition functions; as well as advanced features like the recovery environment (a hidden partition on your main drive that you can boot from to restore), PXE boot (network boot), command line usage, etc. There’s also very affordable cloud storage with the paid version, but it can only be used for Backupper backups, not any other data. Those are all nice features for more advanced users, and if you like the sound of them, read my Aomei Backuppper Professional review. How much is Aomei Backupper Standard 8.5? The only cost associated with Backupper Standard is a small banner ad at the top of the main Window, and a nag to buy the Pro version when you exit the client software. Really, that’s it. Below you can see the retail and discounted prices of the Pro version you’ll see when you surf to the company’s website. Nicely, there’s a perpetual license available for Pro — something no longer available from industry heavyweights such as Acronis True Image and Macrium Reflect X Home. Oddly, there is no mention of the 1TB of online storage (backup and restore only) that is offered with the paid versions for $20/$30 a year. You will find that when you open the “Buy” option from within the trial version of Backupper Professional. Upgrade? To our mind, the Professional version of Backupper adds some nice features, but they’re not necessarily ones that most users need other than the online storage. How does Aomei Backupper Standard 8.5 perform? Backupper Standard ran glitch-free — at least with basic tasks. However, there were a number of non-fatal issues. The major problem, as mentioned twice already, was creating a boot disk that would actually boot — a must-have for disaster recovery. Backupper created the Windows PE ISO just fine, and I was able to use it in VirtualBox, but the USB thumb drive it created did not show up as bootable on my UEFI test bed. I managed to create a bootable USB stick with Rufus 4.8; however, the UEFI in the image was deprecated, so I had to lower the security settings in the BIOS to boot with it. Put bluntly, the recovery media feature is workable if you know the tricks, but hardly ideal. Note that this same boot-disk creation issue plagues the Professional version and has been around since at least version 7. Come on, folks. Once PE recovery media was successfully created, Backupper Standard performed better than fine. It’s not as fast as the Professional version, but it’s hardly slothful either. Most importantly, it finished all backup and restore tasks without error — including a full system restore. I will forgive just about anything if the all-important backup and restore operations work properly. While Backupper Standard restored my system just fine, I suggest you download Macrium Reflect 8 Free as a hedge. My only other, decidedly minor nits are the lack of a “new folder” button when defining some destinations (see above), and having to select network assets by typing in the IP address — there’s no browse function at the point. After you supply the IP address, user name, and password, you can then browse the folders at that location using a standard expandable tree. Hmm. Should you use Aomei Backupper Standard 8.5? Backupper Standard is surprisingly full-featured and offers the reliable (once you manage to create the boot media) disaster recovery that Windows lacks. That it costs you nothing but some time clicking through a nag upon exit is fantastic. However, be sure to create your recovery media (using Rufus) and test it before relying on it for disaster recovery. Also check out the free version of Easeus ToDo Backup or see if you can’t make do with Window’s own File History and the free version of Macrium Reflect. The good news is that users have some solid freebie options to choose from.

item.title: SALES: Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is now available, and it’s built for your toughest tasks
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
Two weeks ago, Google gave Gemini 4 Carbon to a small group of cybersecurity defenders through its Fairwind Program. Now, Carbon is available to developers, businesses, scientists, and Google AI Ultra subscribers. Gemini Argon remains Google’s go-to pick for most coding and office work. Carbon is meant for jobs that push a model to its limits, like complicated debugging or open-ended scientific research. It uses more tokens than Argon, and it spends that extra effort exploring options and verifying its answers. Where does Carbon really shine? The numbers make the strongest case. Carbon ranked first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench, and its cost per task was less than half that of the next best model from another company. - Office documents: Legal and finance teams can feed it dense documents full of charts and tables, and it sticks to strict formatting when building spreadsheets, presentations, and reports. - Web apps: While building an app, Carbon keeps testing its code, recovers when something breaks, and checks how the finished interface looks before wrapping up. - Security: Wiz used it to scan two major SaaS providers, and the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours, a job that would normally take weeks of research. - Lab work: Carbon helped drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio find new toxicity mechanisms its team hadn’t discovered before, and Axiom is now moving its production scientific analyses and agents to Carbon and Argon. Developers also get an early look at /swarm in Google Antigravity. Carbon can take on design, coordination, and reviewing there, while lighter and faster models work on the rest in parallel. Can you try Gemini 4 Carbon today? If you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber, Carbon is rolling out to you in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search, and Google Antigravity. Paying developers and businesses can use it through the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business at Argon’s introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Scientists can apply for a chance at six months of free access to both models, and cybersecurity defenders can apply to the Fairwind Program.

item.title: REVIEW: 8x8 Work Review: A Workhorse VoIP With Powerful Business Features
item.description:
Source: PCMag
8x8 Work ensures dependable voice and video calls for small- and medium-sized businesses looking to make the jump to a unified communications platform. Its interface is simple to use and navigate, and we also like the service's rich reporting tools. That said, the base tier, while affordable, doesn't support third-party integrations or video meetings. Some features, including those related to AI agents and call sentiment, also require add-ons or an expensive plan. Our Editors' Choice winners for VoIP systems remain Intermedia Unite, RingCentral RingEX, and Zoom Phone thanks to their better value and superior user experiences. 8x8 Work's starter X1 plan ($15 per user per month) is meant for companies weaning themselves off a PBX system, so it includes just unlimited voice calling, a multi-level auto-attendant, and call handling features, such as custom voicemail greetings. Some AI features are available with every plan, such as action item generation, summaries, and transcriptions. 8x8 also says all plans support some level of texting, but the usage allowances are too complicated to cover here, so you should reach out to the company for more details if that's important to your business. You have to upgrade to the X2 plan ($25 per user per month) to unlock faxing, chat, and audio and video conferencing. This tier supports voice and video meetings with up to 500 active users, which is excellent. It can store your call and meeting recordings for up to 30 days and allows you to make unlimited international calls to 14 countries. The X2 plan also unlocks various business integrations. I tested the X4 plan ($45 per user per month), which adds more analytics capabilities, introduces call quality reports, and supports calls to 48 countries. It's also the only plan that allows for call barging, monitoring, and whispering. This plan extends recording retention to 130 days. You need to pay for the contact-center-focused Engage plan ($50 per user per month) to unlock sentiment analysis features and a Microsoft Teams integration. For comparison, RingEX's entry-level Core plan ($20 per user per month, billed annually) supports some AI features (real-time call transcriptions and summaries of video meetings), team messaging, text messaging, unlimited domestic calling, and video calls with up to 100 people. Unite Pro ($27.99 per user per month) includes an AI Assistant, business texting, one-to-one and team messaging, unlimited video meetings with up to 100 participants, and unlimited domestic and international calling. Zoom Phone's starting plan ($16 per user per month) also offers both audio calls (unlimited to Canada and the US) and video conferencing, along with a competitive set of AI features. Unite's and Zoom's base tiers also support call barging, whispering, and monitoring. Setting up an account is easy, if a bit time-consuming, thanks to the multiple rounds of authentication. Still, this process helps make the product secure. The next step is to record a greeting for new callers and configure your audio and video settings for calls and meetings. Most of the admin functions are easy to understand and access, with many available both in the browser and in the desktop app. For example, I didn't have any problems finding the voicemail greeting option, recording a take, and activating it for all calls in testing. For more advanced settings related to call handling, faxing, and integrations, you have to navigate to the Account Settings. The options are just as clear here, and I was able to quickly change the call hold music to a spoken-word reminder of what the company does. Setting up the call-handling features was also straightforward, with options to adjust how calls are forwarded, whether they are recorded, and what happens if no one answers (a scenario that could spur hunt groups). Unfortunately, you can't search the Account Settings section for specific settings, so I had to look around a bit for functions related to the automated receptionist and call monitoring. 8x8 Work offers desktop (macOS and Windows) and mobile (Android and iOS) apps, as well as a web version. I tested the iOS and Windows apps, as well as the web experience. All of the platforms are intuitive for everyday calling, messaging, and video conferencing, and I like that the softphone dialer is about as clean as it gets. The clutter-free design makes it easy for you to find the features and settings you need. That said, I wish 8x8 Work's user interface had a little more flair. It offers a dark mode but mostly sticks to a visual design that uses black text on white and gray backgrounds. Both RingEX and Unite use color more effectively to guide you, for example. Like those services, 8x8 Work is full-featured, so it will take time to learn how everything works. Tech support for all users is available 24/7 via chat, email, phone, or a ticket. You can also consult an extensive online help system at any time, too. 8x8 Work offers three dedicated tech support tiers, too, each with a different service level agreement (SLA) on response times. Tier one is for subscriptions totaling under $5,000, tier two is for those totaling between $5,000 and $30,000, and tier three is for those totaling $30,000 per month. I had to hunt around a bit for the online support link in the app (it’s in the far lower left part of the interface), so I wish it were more visually prominent. Nonetheless, when I created a ticket related to login authentication, a rep resolved it within about an hour. The online support form could stand to be simpler, however. You can sync 8x8 Work with your Google or Microsoft contacts to automatically pull them in. For bulk imports via CSV files, you need to head to the settings section (thankfully not the separate admin portal). You then use the 8x8 template, which it clearly lists on the import screen as a download. I had no trouble adding contacts in Google Sheets, saving the file as a CSV, and importing them. 8x8 Work supports a variety of desk phones from brands such as Cisco, Grandstream, Mitel, Poly, Panasonic, and Yealink, as well as ATA adapters (for connecting older analog phones). It also sells a variety of preconfigured devices. Both RingEX and Unite work with a similar number of devices from many of the same brands, but Zoom Phone offers more extensive support. 8x8 says the platform supports about 50 different third-party apps, including Google Workspace, HubSpot, and Salesforce. You can find the full list of integrations here. RingEX, Unite, and Zoom Phone all do better here. 8x8 Work's phone call quality was excellent in testing, and video meetings looked crisp and clear. The latter includes some handy extras, such as breakout rooms and digital whiteboards. You can choose to record phone calls and meetings, and the software automatically informs participants when you do. Small perks and features popped up regularly. For example, during phone calls, you can see a graph displaying call quality (it always rated mine as good). You can also check the analytics dashboard to see how many meetings you held, how long they lasted, and how many people attended over a customizable time period. AI features, such as meeting summaries, benefit from recent improvements. In test calls, 8x8 Work generated accurate transcriptions, clear and helpful meeting summaries, and relevant action items. I even received emails summarizing the meetings. As mentioned, the 8x8 Engage tier unlocks call sentiment analysis. In test calls, I pretended to be an angry customer, and the service accurately identified my negative sentiment in a side panel. Although I didn't test it, the 8x8 AI Studio add-on appears to be a powerful option for larger companies that want to assign AI agents to handle calls and resolve issues. These rely on what the company calls "a reasoning engine" linked to a company knowledge base. Costs vary based on usage and the channels you use. For example, credits for using AI for voice calls are cheaper than those for texting. RingEX takes a similar approach with AI features. You get basic AI-powered transcriptions and summaries with the standard plans, but sentiment analysis and an AI receptionist cost extra. Intermedia Unite can analyze customer sentiment without an add-on, but you must upgrade to a more expensive product to unlock agent sentiment monitoring and coaching, among other things. 8x8 Work includes a full-featured team messaging platform. You can create private or public chat rooms, use emoji, and even communicate with external contacts. File sharing is available through the messaging interface, and I found the experience fluid. You can also share and sync files during meetings. The available analytics tools are powerful and easy to access through a separate tab, but I still wish they were part of the main interface. The dashboard is colorful and well-designed, not purely functional, like the main user experience. 8x8 Work now lets you build custom reports, so I created one on call quality. With one click, it showed me a bright green bar to indicate “excellent” performance for a few calls. The analytics go deeper than what I found in both RingEX and Intermedia Unite, letting me drill into variables such as which calls were not answered at all, device-based call quality, and a ring group summary showing when calls were picked up. 8x8 Work supports multi-factor authentication, and the privacy policy is comprehensive, clear, and even searchable. The product supports end-to-end encryption for calls, meetings, and chats. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Exceptional voice and video meeting quality, combined with granular reporting tools, make 8x8 Work worth considering for your SMB. The service's AI-powered summarization and transcription tools work well, and we like how straightforward the admin settings are. That said, its interface could be livelier, and the voice-focused starting tier isn't as good a value as some competitors' equivalents. RingEx, Unite, and Zoom Phone benefit from more compelling user experiences, a broader range of integrations, and a better distribution of features across plans, so they remain our Editors' Choice winners for the category. It’s a great setup for everyday work, multitasking, and even some creative tasks. Just keep in mind that the 16GB of LPDDR5X RAM is soldered on and can’t be upgraded, so you’ll need to be comfortable with that amount for the long haul. Still, it’s a great desktop piece that not only looks good, but has the power under the hood to back it up as well. What are good websites to find computer deals? There are a ton of sites that sell computers, and scouring through all of them would take you a lot of time—that’s why we do it for you here and highlight the best deals we find. However, to save you some time and frustration, you need to be smart about where you look at any given time of the year. If you’re looking for a new computer during the holidays or around popular sale periods such as Black Friday or back-to-school, then you are likely to find great deals directly through first party vendor websites. These include the retail storefronts of popular computer manufacturers such as HP, Dell, and Lenovo. However, if you are looking in between sales periods, it’s generally a good idea to search through large third-party retailers such as Amazon, Adorama, Walmart, BestBuy, and Newegg. Oftentimes these websites will offer limited Deals of the Day type sales in hopes of getting rid of excess stock. On the upside, you can score still-decent PCs at a steep discount. When’s the best time to shop for a PC computer? Typically you’ll want to time your PC computer shopping around a prominent sales period. The biggest sales periods are Black Friday/Cyber Monday in late November and Amazon Prime Day in early-to-mid July. The best sales often occur leading up to and during these two events and they are great times to snag a new PC computer for cheap. Other holiday shopping periods such as the New Year sales in January, President’s Day sales in February, and the back-to-school sales event in August are also good times to find discounts on computers. What type of desktop should I get? You’ll see a ton of options when searching for a desktop computer, but they all mainly fit into four main categories: productivity tower PCs, gaming PCs, mini PCS, and all-in-ones (AiO). Which you should end up buying is entirely dependent upon what your needs are and what you want to do with your computer. If you are looking for something that will work in a home office or family room, then a productivity PC or AiO with a solid CPU and lots of RAM and storage is probably the way to go. If gaming is your main concern, a gaming PC can offer a lot more bang for your buck than a laptop and you should focus on getting the best GPU possible. Or if you just want something that can fit anywhere and provide basic computing then a mini PC is a good bet. What CPU and GPU should I get? When looking at your new computer’s CPU, get at least an Intel Core i5 or AMD Ryzen 5, both of which will provide plenty of processing power for everyday computing tasks. If you don’t intend to do any PC gaming, then feel free to save some money by going with integrated graphics. However, if you are looking to get your game on, we recommend at least an Nvidia GeForce 3060 or AMD Radeon RX 6600 XT, as these are the least expensive discrete graphics cards that can handle ray tracing well. If you aren’t interested in those cutting-edge lighting effects, however, the RTX 3050 and Radeon RX 6600 also provide decent 1080p gaming performance at even lower prices. The RTX 5070 is a strong midrange card that will allow for high settings at 1440p while the RTX 5080 is capable of decent 4K gaming if that’s more your speed. For those who won’t compromise for anything besides the best, the RTX 5090 is really your only option currently. How much memory and storage does my PC need? As for RAM, we think its best to shoot for 16GB at the minimum for productivity and gaming, but for family computers and internet browsing, 8GB should suffice. Storage size is dependent upon your personal needs, but it is generally a good idea to opt for an SSD over an standard HDD as they are much faster and don’t significantly affect the price of a desktop. Before deciding, it’s best to consider what your intended use of the computer will be. Are you just doing work or web browsing? Then something like 512GB will be plenty. If you want to load up a lot of large files such as games or content creation projects, then you’ll need at least 1 or 2TB or storage. However, just remember that even if your computer doesn’t have enough storage built-in you can always upgrade your SSD or go with an external drive to increase your available storage options. Is it a good idea to buy a refurbished computer? Refurbished computers are used machines that have been repaired, upgraded, and cleaned for the purpose of reselling. They’re usually open-box returns, overstock, or models with minor cosmetic damage (scratches, scuffs, etc). Refurbished computers can be a bargain hunter’s dream as they’re likely still in good (or great) condition and you can save a lot of money. That being said, refurbished computers can have their downsides as well. In addition to cosmetic blemishes, some of the internal components might be a little older or outdated and they might not be in peak condition due to previous usage. If you do consider buying a refurbished computer I recommend looking at eBay as they offer a one-year warranty. You can also check out manufacturer’s retail storefronts like Dell’s Outlet Store and Apple’s Refurbished Store—just be sure to look at the terms of warranty offered before purchasing.

Topdon utilizes image enhancement technology that increases the IR resolution from 256×192 to 512×384, providing a more detailed display with clearer contours, temperature differences, and image information. Five viewing modes are available for various applications: thermal image, thermal fusion, contour fusion, visible light, and picture-in-picture. This allows users to either use the pure thermal image or combine it with visible contours as needed.
